sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the big headline at top left, then the invoice card on the right, then the dark green button. This reads as a SaaS landing page for invoicing, aimed at freelancers and small studios. It feels calm, plain and trustworthy. Job (my assumption): get a freelancer to start the free trial. The image is 1280×800, one screen, so no crops were needed. Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop and entries scripts. I worked from the whole image and my own judgment.

- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this is for? yes
- Do the main image and the headline make one idea? no. The headline promises speed ("time it takes to pour coffee"). The card at about x 892–1231, y 220–416 shows a finished invoice, so it shows the result but not the speed or the auto-fill.
- Does every element and box do a job? no. The three feature cards (y 557–775) are about 220 px tall, but their text ends around y 650. Each card is roughly 60% empty white box.
- Do type, colours and shapes share one mood? yes
- Is the copy finished? yes
- Do repeated elements look the same? yes
- Do colours and shapes carry the mood? yes
- Do headings name their section? yes

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** The three feature cards span about y 557–775 at x 25–418, 444–836 and 862–1255. Their heading and one or two lines of text stop around y 600–650, so about 125 px of each card is empty white box. Viewers read the empty lower halves as missing content: an image that didn't load, or a section that isn't finished. That makes the page look less finished right where it should be backing up the hero's claims. The cards also take up the whole lower third and push nothing further down into view. Direction: either fill each card with something that proves its claim (a sample reminder email, a two-tap payment view, a report preview) or shrink the cards to fit their text and use the freed space to show more of the page. If the cards are meant to hold images that didn't render in this capture, check that in a live browser. Common sense, no catalog source checked. **Defect, major.**
2. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** The headline at x 48–625, y 170–335 promises speed, and the subhead promises auto-fill and chasing late payments. The invoice card at about x 892–1231, y 220–416 is a static, finished invoice that any invoicing tool could show. Nothing in it shows that it took seconds, that fields filled themselves, or that a reminder went out. So viewers have to take the coffee claim on trust. The picture adds "this makes invoices" and nothing more, and the specific promise goes unshown. Direction: make the visual carry the speed or auto-fill claim. For example, show fields marked as filled in for you, or a "sent in 0:41" or "reminder scheduled" state, so the picture proves what the headline says. The large empty area of the green panel between the copy and the card (about x 640–890) has room for this. **Taste, major.**

**What's working.** 
- One mood holds across the whole piece. The warm off-white page, the sage hero panel, the deep green button and the soft rounded white cards all belong together and feel calm, which suits a tool that promises to take a chore off your hands. 
- The copy is concrete and specific. "Send an invoice in the time it takes to pour coffee" uses an everyday comparison, "Start free for 14 days" names one exact action, and each card heading says what the feature does ("Reports for tax time").

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty lower halves of the feature cards are meant to hold images or animations that hadn't loaded when the screenshot was taken. Check this in a live browser.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; every element does a job)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was denied. The image looks to be about 1280×800, a single screen, so the script would have printed `no crops` and I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on the headline "Send an invoice in the time it takes to pour coffee." Next it goes to the invoice card on the right, then the dark green "Start free for 14 days" button. Last, it drops to the three feature cards. This reads as a landing page for a small-business invoicing tool, aimed at freelancers and small studios. It feels calm and tidy.

Assumed job: get a freelancer to understand the product and start the free trial.

What matters first:
- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? **Yes.** The headline is about 56 px, heavy and near-black, far bigger than anything else.
- Below the first element, can you tell each level from the next, with no two sizes almost the same? **Yes.** The levels are the headline (about 56 px), the lede (about 18 px, regular, grey), the card headings (about 17 px, semibold, dark) and the body and invoice rows (about 14 px, grey). The lede and the card headings are almost the same size, but weight and colour separate them, and they sit in different regions with different roles. They read as distinct at a glance.
- Where headings are clearly larger than the text, do they also differ in weight, form or color? **Yes.** The headline and card headings are bold and dark; the body is regular and grey.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline is the one clear place to start.** At about 56 px, heavy weight and near-black on pale sage (x 48–625, y 170–340), it is roughly three times the size of the next text. The eye has no competition for where to begin, and it moves on to the invoice card and then the button in a sensible order.
- **Lower levels are told apart by weight and colour, not just size.** The feature headings ("Reminders that sound human", y ≈ 593) are close in size to the lede (≈ 18 px vs ≈ 17 px). They still read as a different level because they are semibold and dark while the lede is regular and grey. This is the "bolder, not bigger" approach from Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*. Keep it if the type is revised; matching the lede's weight to the card headings would blur the two levels.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** The answer is no. Each of the three feature cards (y≈557–775) has its title and one or two lines of text in the top ~90 px. Below that sit about 120 px of empty white, with the bottom border closing it off. That is the bottom quarter of the first screen. The empty space here isn't shaped to give the eye a rest. It is left over inside three boxes, so the cards look unfinished, as if a picture or a link failed to load. Ruder's point is that empty space should be set against dense areas on purpose (*Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts", "Form and counter-form"). These cards hold no dense area for the space to work against. If there is meant to be an illustration or a "Learn more" link at the bottom of each card, the space is fine once it's there. Otherwise, fit the card height to its content, or fill the cards so the text and the space each take a clear share. Taste/convention (Ruder), minor.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** The answer is no, though only just. In the hero (x 24–1256, y 104–531), the three-line headline is very large and near-black, and it takes up the whole left half (x 48–625). The right half is mostly empty mint. Its only counterweight is the invoice card (about 340×197 px at x 892–1231), which is pale with small text. The card's isolation adds some weight, but not enough, so the hero leans left. That leaves the product proof looking like an afterthought next to the claim. Arnheim notes that a heavy side needs a counterweight (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Fix: give the right side more mass. Enlarge the invoice so it fills more of the right column and moves toward the text, or add depth to it (a status, a "Paid" state, a layered second card). Taste, minor.

**What's working.**
- **One strict grid:** The outer edges sit at x=24/1256 and the content edges at x=48/1232. They line up down the nav, the hero and the cards, which have equal ~25 px gutters, and "Sign in" lines up with the right edge of the invoice card. Nothing looks placed by eye, which is why the page reads calm and trustworthy.
- **Vertical centring with purpose:** The invoice card is centred vertically on the hero's text block (headline to button, centre ≈ y 318). The two halves sit on one axis without stacking everything on a central line.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (empty space gathered; visual weight balances), 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The hero headline (about x 48–625, y 170–340) breaks as "Send an invoice in the / time it takes to pour / coffee." The first line ends on "the", which splits it from its noun "time", so the first line reads as a fragment and the reader has to carry the article over the break. The last line holds only "coffee.", which leaves the punchline alone and makes the block look unbalanced against the full lines above it. The subhead (y 355–405) also breaks inside a phrase, at "late / payments", which splits the adjective from its noun. The cause is the box width deciding the breaks, not the sense of the words. Break by phrase instead, for example "Send an invoice / in the time it takes / to pour coffee." Do this with manual breaks or `text-wrap: balance` on the headline, and narrow or widen the subhead's measure so "late payments" stays on one line. This is a convention, from the "Line breaks in headings and short text" entry in references/typography.md. I couldn't open the entry because the entries script was refused, so this rests on the checklist line itself. **Minor**: the headline still reads fine, but at this size and position it is the most-read text on the page.

**What's working.**
- **The invoice card's numbers are right.** $640.00 + $45.00 + 8% tax ($54.80) adds up to $739.80, and every amount sits on one right edge at about x 1211. A product that promises to fill in your rates and tax shows a sum the viewer can check and find correct. Keep the figures right-aligned and tabular.
- **The type follows one plan.** It all looks like one sans family (Inter or similar) in plain upright weights. The sizes have clear jobs: a roughly 60 px bold headline, an 18 px grey subhead, 16 px semibold card titles, and 14 px grey body and nav text. Leading is tight on the headline and open in the paragraphs. Body text in the feature cards is no smaller than the nav and runs well under 75 characters.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the headline and subhead break at other viewport widths. The breaks above come from this box width, so check them at common desktop and mobile widths after any fix.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One strong color, used once.** The deep green on "Start free for 14 days" (48–255, 420–468) is the only saturated color on the page. Everything else is cream, white, pale sage, gray or near-black, so the eye goes straight from the headline to the button. No other color competes with the button for attention (Refactoring UI, accent restraint).
- **Structure comes from lightness, not hue.** The near-black headline, the dark button and the white invoice card on sage all differ clearly in lightness, so the hierarchy still holds in grayscale. One weak spot that I did not count as a fault: the sage hero (24–1256, 104–532) and the cream page are nearly the same lightness, so in grayscale the panel's edge almost disappears. The same goes for the white feature cards on cream (y 556–776), which are held up only by their thin beige borders. None of the content merges, so the hierarchy holds. If the designer wants the panels to read as separate blocks, a slightly darker hero tint would do it (Albers; Refactoring UI).

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

The pictures walk:

- Line 1, every image shows its content with no empty placeholder: **no**. Each of the three feature cards (about x 25–1255, y 557–775) has a blank lower half of about 120 px below its text (y ~655–775). That is the shape of an image slot whose picture didn't load or was never added.
- Line 2, full quality: yes. The only marks are the "Tallyfold" wordmark and the invoice mockup, and both are crisp.
- Line 3, crops look intended: yes. Nothing is cropped.
- Line 4, subject stands apart from background: yes. The white invoice card stands clear of the pale green hero.
- Line 5, one rendering style: yes. The only depicted object is the flat invoice card.
- Lines 6–8, photos, icons/line drawings, one viewpoint and light: yes. There are no photos, no icons and no scenes.
- Line 9, texture and pattern: yes. There is none.
- Line 10, honest surfaces: yes. The surfaces are flat, with no fake bevels or depth.
- Line 11, logo clear space, undistorted, own colors: yes. The wordmark at 48,52 has ample space in the nav bar.
- Line 12, logo simple enough small and in one color: yes. It is a plain bold wordmark.

Line 1 has no catalog entry, so there are no entries to open. I judged it by common sense.

**Section.** Pictures: applies, narrowly. The page has no photos, illustrations or icons. The only picture-like elements are the "Tallyfold" wordmark (about x 48–132, y 52), the invoice mockup card in the hero (about x 893–1231, y 220–416), and three empty bands in the feature cards that look like missing images.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No.
   - **Where:** In all three feature cards ("Reminders that sound human", "Pay by card or transfer", "Reports for tax time"; y 557–775), the text ends by about y 650 in the first card and about y 630 in the other two. Below that is about 120–145 px of empty white, the same in each card.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The cards look unfinished, like slots waiting for a screenshot or illustration that never arrived. The viewer reads the space as a loading failure or a template left half-filled, and that undercuts a product that sells polish ("reminders that sound human"). The three features also get no visual proof. The hero mockup shows the product, but these cards only make claims.
   - **Why:** No catalog entry covers this, so this is my common-sense judgment. Uniform empty space at the bottom of matching cards reads as a missing asset, not as breathing room.
   - **Fix direction:** If images were meant to go there, check that they load. A small product vignette in the same flat style as the hero invoice would work: a reminder email, the pay button, an export file. If no images were meant, shrink the cards to fit their text so the empty space stops looking like a slot.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect if the images failed to load, taste if the empty space was on purpose. Major: it is the whole lower third of the first screen and makes the page look unfinished.

**What's working.**
- **The hero invoice mockup works as a picture.** It shows a real invoice with real line items and a total, so the product's promise becomes concrete in one glance. It is flat, crisp, and stands clearly off the green panel. Keep this approach, and if pictures go in the feature cards, draw them in the same style.
- **The wordmark is a plain bold "Tallyfold".** It has clean clear space in the nav, so it will survive at small sizes and in one color.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the feature cards' empty space is an image that failed to load. Check the page in a live browser and look for failed image requests in the network panel.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content, no empty placeholder box)

This looks like a landing page for invoicing software for freelancers and small businesses. The only data is the invoice card at x≈893–1231, y≈220–416. It is a small table of figures, so the section applies, but most chart lines don't apply to a table and count as yes.
- Form fits data (table for exact values): yes
- Series followable: yes (none)
- Ink mostly data: yes (a single hairline above the total, no grid)

- Time range: yes (n/a)
- Palette fits: yes (n/a)
- Not color alone: yes
- Few colors: yes
- Labels at data: yes (each label sits on its own row, no legend)
- Names units: yes ($, "200 units", "8%")
- Labels clear: yes
- Finding in words: yes (the headline next to it carries the point)
- Sorted: yes (invoice order: items, delivery, tax, total)
- Estimates marked: yes (none)

- Dashboard fits: yes (n/a)

No lines answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Charts and data: applies. The only data is the sample invoice table in the hero.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The invoice card works as a table of exact values.** It sits at about x 893–1231, y 220–416. Labels are left-aligned and the amounts are right-aligned in one column, so the decimal points line up. One thin rule sets off a bold "Total due $739.80". There's no grid, shading or other chrome, so nearly all the ink in the card is data.
- **The numbers add up.** $640 + $45 = $685, 8% tax on that is $54.80, and the total is $739.80. Every figure has its unit ($, "200 units", "8%"). A viewer who checks the sum finds it's right, which supports the product's claim that it "fills in your clients, rates, and tax." If the sum were wrong, it would undercut that promise.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 16 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has top navigation (Product, Pricing, Guides, Sign in) and one call-to-action button. There are no forms, dialogs or states.

**Findings**
None. Every checklist line is yes, apart from the two focus lines, which a still image can't show.

One copy note that no Interface line covers, for the director to weigh. The button "Start free for 14 days" (48,420 to 255,467) is the one thing on the page that commits the viewer, but nothing near it says what happens on day 15. It could mean "you'll be charged automatically unless you cancel" or "the trial stops and nothing is billed." Nothing in this 800 px view says whether a card is needed either. A wary freelancer will stop at the button to find out. To fix it, put a short line under the button, such as "No card needed" or "Cancel any time before day 15." This is a defect under "the words are part of the design", but minor, and fine print further down the page might already cover it.

**What's working.**
- **Only one button.** "Start free for 14 days" is the only filled button: white bold text on dark green over a pale green panel. "Sign in" at the top right is plain text, so returning users can find it without it competing with the trial offer. That is the right primary/secondary split (Refactoring UI; NN/g on primary versus secondary actions).
- **Standard header.** Logo on the left, three short nav links next to it and Sign in on the far right is the layout visitors expect from SaaS sites (Jakob's law). The links are about 28 px apart, so even as text-only links they look clear of the 24 px target minimum (WCAG 2.5.8).

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Focus.** Whether the button and nav links show a visible focus ring with 3:1 contrast. Check the dark green button on the pale green panel in a live browser, because a focus ring in a similar green would disappear there.
- **Feature cards.** Whether the three cards are links. They are large bordered white boxes, so people may try to click them. If they're not links, that's fine; if they are, they need a visible sign that they can be clicked.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 0 no, 2 unsure (focus indicator visible at 2 px and 3:1; focused control not obscured)
